newsitem.title: JAPAN: SPEED SKATING-NEW SPEED FROM OLD-STYLE SKATES.
newsitem.headline: SPEED SKATING-NEW SPEED FROM OLD-STYLE SKATES.

text.p: A century-old skate design has swept the speed-skating world this winter.

About two-thirds of the 34 women competing at the world championships this weekend and a third of the 45 male competitors are expected to use the new "slap" skates, which release at the heel, said Dutch coaching co-ordinator Ab Krook.
The skates can slice up to six seconds off a skater's 3,000-metre time, he added.

The original patent for the design, issued to a German inventor in 1894, failed to attract much attention until an updated version was pioneered earlier this winter on the World Cup circuit by Dutch women skaters.
After Tonny de Jong of the Netherlands replaced Germany's Gunda Niemann as the world's top women's long-distance skater, competitors hurriedly began switching to the Dutch-made Viking skates.
Using the new skates, Niemann led a German sweep of the women's 3,000 metres at the last World Cup event in Davos, Switzerland.

"We made the decision we had to do it, we had to change," said German team chief Helmut Kraus, who added that Germany first asked the International Skating Union (ISU) if the new skates would be allowed at next year's Winter Olympics in Nagano.
ISU regulations specify only that blades cannot be heated with any mechanical device, Jan Charisius, chairman of the ISU's speed-skating committee, said.
"There is no problem (using the skates) for the Olympics," he said.
Charisius added that the ISU would not make any rule changes until its post-Olympic congress in 1998: "We need a definition of what a skate is."
Slap skates are made so that the boot heel separates and rises from the blade when the skater pushes against the ice, allowing a more natural stride than with rigid conventional skates.
The blade slaps back to the heel when the foot is lifted off the ice.
Krook said Dutch junior skaters had experimented with the skates for four years and similar models had been available in Dutch shops since 1985 but top-level speed skaters were reluctant to try them.
"When you are the best in the world, it's a big risk to change your skates," Krook said. "Even when people get a new pair of normal skates, they can have problems adjusting."

Viking has offered slap skates free to all international competitors to ensure that no country has an unfair advantage but demand for skates during Europe's unusually cold winter has depleted stocks for ordinary buyers.

So far, more women than men have taken up Viking's offer as heavier skaters sometimes find them unstable. The skates are most helpful in maintaining speed in longer races rather than gaining speed in sprints.
"It's the future and we must try these skates," Russia's Svetlana Bazhanova, gold medallist in the 3,000 metres at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics, said.
She gave the skates a second try at Davos after breaking her first pair and returning briefly to conventional skates.

Others are less enthusiastic about the change. "It's not speed skating," Kraus said. "With the old skates you can see and hear the dynamics of skating a little more. With the slap skate you can only hear the plop, plop."

Speed skating has too few competitors to adopt cross-country skiing's solution to a similar problem, he said. After skiers started using skating techniques, separate races were offered for classic and free techniques.
Despite his reservations, Kraus knows that slap skates are just the beginning of innovations in speed-skating technology.
Turbo skates might be the next development, he suggested. "I'm joking," he added. "We don't have enough money to develop something like that but there's nothing in the rules to prevent it."
